source_text: Sed enim quanta vis est perversitatis ad fidem labefactandam, vel in totum non recipiendam, ut ex his eam impugnet, ex quibus constat. Nihil adeo est quod tam obduret mentes hominum, quam simplicitas divinorum operum quae in actu videtur, et magnificentia quae in effectu repromittitur: ut hic quoque, quoniam tanta simplicitate sine pompa, sine apparatu novo aliquo, denique sine sumptu homo in aqua demissus, et inter pauca verba tinctus, non multo vel nihilo mundior resurgit, eo incredibilis existimetur consecutio aeternitatis. Mentior, si non e contrario idolorum solemnia vel arcana, de suggestu et apparatu, deque sumptu, fidem et auctoritatem sibi exstruunt. Pro! misera incredulitas, quae denegas Deo proprietates suas, simplicitatem et potestatem. Quid ergo? nonne mirandum et lavacro dilui mortem? Atquin eo magis credendum, si, quia mirandum est, idcirco non creditur. Qualia enim decet esse opera divina, nisi super omnem admirationem? Nos quoque ipsi miramur, sed quia credimus. Caeterum incredulitas miratur, non credit. Miratur enim simplicia quasi vana, magnifica quasi impossibilia. Et sit plane ut putas, satis ad utrumque divina pronuntiatio praecucurrit: Stulta mundi elegit Deus ut confundat sapientiam ejus, et Praedifficitia penes homines, facilia penes Deum. Nam si Deus et sapiens et potens, quod etiam praetereuntes eum non negant, merito in adversariis sapientiae potentiaeque, id est in stultitia et impossibilitate materias operationis suae instituit. Quoniam virtus omnis ex his caussam accipit, a quibus provocatur.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed how great is the force of perversity for undermining faith, or for not receiving it at all, so that from those things from which it consists, it attacks it. There is nothing which so hardens the minds of men as the simplicity of divine works which is seen in action, and the magnificence which is promised in effect: so that here also, since with such great simplicity, without pomp, without new apparatus, finally without expense, a man is immersed in water, and among few words is dipped, and rises up not much or not at all cleaner, the consequence of eternity is considered incredible. I lie, if on the contrary, the solemnities or mysteries of idols do not establish faith and authority for themselves from stage and apparatus, and from expense. Away! wretched incredulity, which denies to God His own properties, simplicity and power. What then? Is it not to be wondered at, that death is washed away by washing? But all the more it is to be believed, if, because it is to be wondered at, it is not believed. For what kind of works ought divine works to be, if not beyond all wonder? We also ourselves wonder, but because we believe. On the other hand, incredulity wonders, does not believe. For it wonders at simple things as if they were vain, at magnificent things as if they were impossible. And let it be, as you think, the divine pronouncement has preceded sufficiently for both: God has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound its wisdom, and the weak things, which are easy with God. For if God is both wise and powerful, which even those passing by Him do not deny, rightly in the adversaries of wisdom and power, that is in foolishness and impossibility, He has established the materials of His operation. Since all virtue takes its cause from those things by which it is provoked.

pass_b_english: But consider the sheer force of perversity: it aims to undermine faith or reject it outright, turning the very evidence that establishes faith into weapons against it. Nothing hardens human minds like the simplicity of divine works seen in action, and the magnificence promised in their effect. Here, too, because a man is plunged into water with such stark simplicity — no pomp, no novel apparatus, ultimately no expense — dipped amid a few words, and rises no cleaner than before, the promise of eternity strikes people as incredible. I am lying if the solemnities and mysteries of idols do not, by contrast, build their own credibility and authority on spectacle, stagecraft, and expense. Away with it, this wretched unbelief that denies God his own properties: simplicity and power. So what? Is it not a wonder that death is washed away by washing? Yet all the more it must be believed precisely because it is wonderful enough to be disbelieved. What kind of works should divine works be, if not beyond all wonder? We ourselves wonder, but we wonder because we believe. Unbelief, on the other hand, wonders and refuses to believe. It treats simple things as empty, magnificent things as impossible. And let it stand as you suppose: the divine pronouncement has already raced ahead to cover both points. God chose the foolish things of the world to shame its wisdom (1 Cor. 1:27), and the weak things — what is easy for God. For if God is both wise and powerful, which even passersby do not deny, he rightly establishes the materials of his operation in the opponents of wisdom and power — that is, in foolishness and impossibility. Since all power draws its cause from the very things that provoke it.
